name: Benny Paret
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Undisputed World Welterweight Championship on May 27, 1960, by defeating Don Jordan, and recaptured it on September 30, 1961.
early_history_summary: Paret began his professional boxing career in 1954 at age 17, accumulating a record of 35 wins, 12 losses, and 3 draws over eight years. He won the world welterweight title at age 23 and defended it in high-profile bouts against Emile Griffith and Gene Fullmer before his death at 25 from injuries sustained in a 1962 title fight.
primary_leverage_engine: Physical talent and early professional reps
family_context_summary: Born in Santa Clara, Cuba; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Cuban boxing pipeline, early professional immersion, physical talent
evidence_summary: Paret turned professional at 17 in 1954, fighting 50 bouts over eight years and winning the world welterweight title at 23. Cuba had a strong boxing culture that provided a pipeline for young fighters. His manager Manuel Alfaro guided his career. Family background is not documented. He died at 25 from injuries in a televised title defense against Emile Griffith, making his career short but historically significant.
starting_point: Born in Santa Clara, Cuba in 1937; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Died April 3, 1962 at age 25 from brain hemorrhaging sustained in a March 24, 1962 title defense against Emile Griffith at Madison Square Garden.

trajectory.event: Began professional boxing career with his debut on April 16, 1954.
Won the Undisputed World Welterweight Championship by defeating Don Jordan on May 27.
Lost title to Emile Griffith in April, then recaptured it in a split-decision on September 30.
Died on April 3 from brain injuries sustained in a March 24 title defense against Emile Griffith, televised live on ABC.

His first notable building was a restaurant in Berhida in 1964 (age 28), and his first internationally recognized work was the Sárospatak Cultural Center in 1972 (age 36). name: Abebe Bikila
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. His Olympic gold medal at the 1960 Rome Olympics was won at age 28. Before that, he finished second in the Ethiopian Armed Forces championship in 1956 at age 24, which is not a material international milestone.
family_context_summary: Born in Jato, Shewa, Ethiopia; son of Wudinesh Beneberu and her second husband Demissie. Rural farming family. Family displaced during the Second Italo-Ethiopian War.
evidence_summary: Bikila was born in rural Ethiopia in 1932 and joined the Ethiopian Imperial Guard around 1952 at age 19-20. He was trained by Swedish coach Onni Niskanen and finished second in the Ethiopian Armed Forces championship in 1956 at age 24. His first marathon win was in July 1960 at age 28, followed by his iconic barefoot Olympic gold at Rome in September 1960. No material milestone by age 26 was found; his fame arrived at 28.

name: Jan Boklöv
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 1988-89 Ski Jumping World Cup overall title at age 22-23, popularizing the V-style technique that revolutionized the sport.
early_history_summary: Boklöv began ski jumping as a youth in Koskullskulle, northern Sweden, winning Swedish national championships from 1985 (age 19). He discovered the V-style by accident during training in the mid-1980s when wind separated his skis, adding 20 meters to his jump. He won his first World Cup competition on December 10, 1988 in Lake Placid using the V-style, and dominated the 1988-89 season with five individual wins to claim the overall World Cup title.
family_context_summary: Born in Koskullskulle, Gällivare, Sweden; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: northern Sweden ski culture, early facility access, V-style innovation, trainer Kurt Elimä
evidence_summary: Boklöv grew up in Koskullskulle, Gällivare in northern Sweden, a region with ski jumping tradition. He won Swedish national championships from age 19 in 1985. He accidentally discovered the V-style technique during training and systematically developed it, winning his first World Cup in December 1988 and the overall World Cup title in 1988-89 at age 22-23. Trainer Kurt Elimä guided his development. Family background is not documented.
starting_point: Born in Koskullskulle, Gällivare, Sweden in 1966; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Former Swedish ski jumper who won the 1988-89 World Cup overall title and revolutionized the sport by popularizing the V-style; reportedly lived in Luxembourg in the early 2000s.

trajectory.event: Won Swedish national championship in ski jumping (normal hill), marking emergence on the national scene.
Won his first World Cup competition in Lake Placid on December 10 using the V-style technique.
Won the 1988-89 Ski Jumping World Cup overall title with five individual victories; received the Jerringpriset as Sweden's best sports performance of the year.
Competed at the Winter Olympics in Albertville, finishing 47th in individual normal hill and 7th in team large hill.
Ended his World Cup career after the 1992-93 season.

name: Petr Korda
milestone_by_age_26: Won the boys' doubles title at the 1985 French Open with Cyril Suk at age 17, reaching joint-World No. 1 junior doubles ranking; won first professional doubles title in 1988 and first singles title in 1991, all by age 23.
early_history_summary: Korda emerged from the Czechoslovakian tennis system as a promising junior, winning the boys' doubles at the 1985 French Open at age 17. He turned professional in 1987 and won his first doubles title in 1988 at age 20, followed by his first singles title in 1991 at age 23. He reached the French Open singles final in 1992 at age 24.
family_context_summary: Born in Prague, Czechoslovakia; family background not documented in reviewed sources. Married former professional tennis player Regina Rajchrtová.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Czechoslovakian tennis system, junior Grand Slam, doubles partnership, early pro immersion
evidence_summary: Korda came through the Czechoslovakian tennis pipeline, winning the boys' doubles at the 1985 French Open at 17 with partner Cyril Suk. He turned pro in 1987, won his first doubles title at 20 and first singles title at 23. The Czech tennis system provided structured training and competition. Family background is not documented. He later won the 1998 Australian Open and reached world No. 2 before a doping ban.
starting_point: Born in Prague, Czechoslovakia in 1968; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Former Czech tennis player ranked world No. 2 in 1998; father of professional golfers Jessica and Nelly Korda and tennis player Sebastian Korda; resides in Monte Carlo and Bradenton, Florida.

trajectory.event: Won boys' doubles title at the French Open with Cyril Suk; ranked joint-World No. 1 junior doubles player.
Won his first career ATP doubles title.
Won his first top-level ATP singles title.
Reached the French Open singles final, losing to defending champion Jim Courier in straight sets.
Won the Australian Open singles title, defeating Marcelo Ríos in straight sets; reached career-high ranking of world No. 2.
Banned for 12 months by the ITF after testing positive for nandrolone at Wimbledon 1998; retired from professional tennis.

name: Alan Jones
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. At age 26 (1972-1973), Jones was competing in British Formula Three, winning six races in 1973 but losing the championship. His first Formula One race was at age 28 (1975), first F1 win at 30 (1977), and World Championship at 33 (1980).
family_context_summary: Born in Melbourne, Australia; son of Stan Jones, an Australian racing driver who won the 1959 Australian Grand Prix and owned a Holden dealership. Jones attended Xavier College.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Stan Jones was a successful Australian racing driver and Holden dealership owner who won the 1959 Australian Grand Prix, providing direct domain exposure and racing culture immersion from childhood.
evidence_summary: Jones grew up immersed in racing through his father Stan Jones, a top Australian racer and Holden dealer. He went to Europe in 1967 at age 20 but couldn't afford Formula Ford. He returned to the UK in 1970 and competed in Formula Three, winning his first race in 1971 at age 24. In 1973 at age 26-27, he won six F3 races and led the championship but lost due to engine failure. His F1 debut came at 28 in 1975. While his F3 results at 26 are documented, they represent a feeder-series achievement, not a material career milestone.

name: Xi Mingze

name: Wilson Fittipaldi Júnior
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Won numerous Brazilian national endurance races from 1963-1968 (ages 19-25) and a British Formula Three race at Silverstone in 1970 at age 26, but these are regional/feeder-level achievements. His Formula One debut came at age 28 in 1972.
family_context_summary: Born in São Paulo, Brazil; son of Wilson Fittipaldi Sr., a journalist, broadcaster, and motorsport enthusiast who founded the Mil Milhas race. Mother Jozefa was of Russian descent. Both parents raced production cars after WWII. Brother of F1 champion Emerson Fittipaldi.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a motorsport journalist and broadcaster who founded the Mil Milhas Brasileiras endurance race; both parents raced production cars. Deep family immersion in motorsport culture.
evidence_summary: Fittipaldi grew up in a motorsport family in São Paulo; his father was a journalist who founded the Mil Milhas race and both parents raced cars. He and brother Emerson built karts and Formula Vee cars in their teens, financing their early careers through a custom car accessory business. Wilson won Brazilian national races from 1963-1968 and a British F3 race at Silverstone in 1970 at age 26, but his F1 debut came at 28 in 1972. No material milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Doutzen Kroes
milestone_by_age_26: Featured on the cover of Vogue Italia in 2005 at age 20 shot by Steven Meisel, voted Model of the Year on Vogue.com; became L'Oréal Paris brand ambassador in 2006 at 21 and Victoria's Secret Angel in 2008 at 23.
early_history_summary: Kroes grew up in the small village of Eastermar in Friesland, Netherlands, aspiring to be a speed skater like her parents. She sent holiday photos to Paparazzi Model Management in Amsterdam in 2003 at age 18 and was signed. Her agency sent her to New York where she was quickly cast by Victoria's Secret. Her breakthrough came in 2005 with the Vogue Italia cover shot by Steven Meisel.

family_context_summary: Born in Eastermar, Friesland, Netherlands; mother Geartsje Leistra was a nurse then teacher, father Johan Kroes was a psychotherapist. Both were champion speed skaters in the 1970s. Has a younger sister Rens who is a nutritionist.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were champion speed skaters, not involved in fashion or modeling; no domain advantage transferred to modeling career.
primary_early_advantage_tags: natural modeling appearance, height, Vogue Italia cover, Victoria's Secret, L'Oréal
evidence_summary: Kroes was born in a small Frisian village to parents who were champion speed skaters but had no fashion connections. She sent snapshots to Paparazzi Model Management in Amsterdam in 2003 at age 18 and was signed without being scouted. Her agency sent her to New York where Steven Meisel shot her Vogue Italia cover in 2005 at age 20, launching her to top-model status. She became a L'Oréal ambassador at 21 and Victoria's Secret Angel at 23, becoming one of the world's highest-paid models. Her physical appearance was the primary driver of her rapid ascent.

current_position: Dutch fashion model and actress; former Victoria's Secret Angel (2008-2014); L'Oréal Paris brand ambassador since 2006; estimated net worth ~€29 million; married to DJ Sunnery James Gorré with two children; resides in Amsterdam.

Became brand ambassador for L'Oréal Paris, a long-standing contract.

Ranked second on Forbes top-earning models list with estimated $8 million in annual earnings; ended Victoria's Secret contract.
Appeared in the superhero film Wonder Woman as Amazon warrior Venelia.

name: Jeff Wall
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Wall was included in the 1970 Information exhibition at MoMA at age 23-24, but then stopped making art entirely from 1970 to 1977. His first back-lit photo-transparency (the medium he is famous for) was made in 1977 at age 30-31, and his first major work The Destroyed Room was in 1978.
family_context_summary: Born in Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada; parents encouraged his interest in art. His first studio was a converted toolshed in the backyard of his family home.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents encouraged early interest in art; father's occupation not documented. Family provided a backyard shed for painting as a teenager.
evidence_summary: Wall grew up in Vancouver with parents who encouraged his art interest; he painted from age 14 in a backyard shed. He received his BA from UBC in 1968 and MA in 1970, and was included in the MoMA's Information exhibition in 1970 at age 23-24. However, he then stopped making art entirely for seven years. His first back-lit photo-transparency was made in 1977 at age 30-31, and his first major work The Destroyed Room was exhibited in 1978. The MoMA inclusion was a group show of conceptual art as a student, not a career-defining milestone. No material milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Jörgen Persson
milestone_by_age_26: Won the European Championship in Men's Singles in 1986 at age 20, and the World Championship in Men's Singles in 1991 at age 25, beating Jan-Ove Waldner in the final and reaching World No. 1 ranking.
early_history_summary: Persson started playing table tennis at age 5 against his parents' bedroom door in Halmstad, Sweden, and began training properly at age 7 when discovered by a coach from Halmstad Bordtennisklubb. At age 14 in 1980, he won the cadet boys' singles at the European Youth Championships, beating Jan-Ove Waldner. He became European Champion in Men's Singles in 1986 at age 20 and World Champion in 1991 at age 25.
family_context_summary: Born in Halmstad, Sweden; started playing table tennis at age 5 against his parents' bedroom door. Father was involved and gave him advice on competing against friends.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was engaged in his table tennis development and gave strategic advice about competing, including not practicing with final opponents before major matches.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Halmstad BK, Swedish table tennis golden era, Waldner rivalry, early start age 5, European cadet champion at 14
evidence_summary: Persson began playing table tennis at age 5 in Halmstad, Sweden, and was discovered by a coach from Halmstad Bordtennisklubb at age 7. He won the European cadet title at 14 in 1980, beating future rival Jan-Ove Waldner. Sweden was then a table tennis powerhouse with role models like Stellan Bengtsson nearby. He became European Champion at 20 in 1986 and World Champion at 25 in 1991, both achieved in the context of Sweden's golden era alongside Waldner. His father provided strategic advice throughout his career.
starting_point: Born in Halmstad, Sweden in 1966; started playing table tennis at age 5 against his parents' bedroom door before being discovered by a local club coach at age 7.
current_position: Former Swedish table tennis player, World Champion (1991) and World No. 1 (1991-1992); competed in seven Olympic Games from 1988 to 2012; retired after the 2012 London Olympics.

trajectory.event: Won the cadet boys' singles at the European Youth Championships in Poznan, beating Jan-Ove Waldner in the final.

Placed 4th at the Beijing Olympics, a remarkable result at age 42.
Competed in his seventh Olympic Games in London; officially retired from competitive table tennis.
